lines.text: Astronomers may have just found a new dwarf planet, hiding beyond Pluto.
For now, it's called 2026 ED138. It was spotted with the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile.
Astronomer Matthew Holman found it on October 13, in Rubin images taken since March.
Why did nobody see it before? It sits near the plane of the Milky Way, lost among millions of stars. Rubin picked it out by its slow motion.
Right now, it's about 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth is. One trip around the Sun takes roughly 280 years.
Its size is still uncertain: somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometres across. Pluto is about 2,377.
If it's confirmed, it would join just five official dwarf planets: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
Next, other telescopes will try to measure its true size. Our solar system may still be hiding more worlds.
